overview: Afanasevo, often spelled Afanasievo, names related early herding communities known through archaeology across the Altai, Minusinsk Basin and adjoining regions. It was not a single state. This map repeats a broad outline from 3000 to 1500 BCE, well beyond the principal dated Afanasievo phases. Some discoveries also lie outside its simplified boundary.

periods.title: Early herding communities
periods.summary: The map catches part of a longer late-fourth- and third-millennium archaeological sequence; radiocarbon dates differ between regions.

periods.title: Later map coverage
periods.summary: Okunev and other regional traditions developed while the atlas continues displaying Afanasevo. This interval is not evidence of one culture remaining unchanged.

items.text: Afanasievo communities helped carry livestock management across a vast region toward Mongolia. Research considers both migrating people and the spread of practices between neighbors. Local East Asian communities also contributed innovations to later pastoral life. The achievement was a far-reaching change in how people obtained food, rather than the creation of an empire stretching across the map.

A 2018 radiocarbon review placed its core Altai burial dates in the thirty-first to twenty-ninth centuries BCE and Middle Yenisei dates in the twenty-ninth to twenty-fifth centuries BCE. Older wood and less precise methods had helped produce longer chronologies. The authors called these results a core that further research could expand, not a final timetable for every community.

At Nizhnyaya Sooru beside the Karakol River, genetic analysis identified all five tested animal teeth as domestic sheep. Two were radiocarbon dated, supporting activity roughly 3300-2900 BCE, partly before this map begins. These teeth provide direct evidence of managed livestock in a settlement, rather than relying solely on the appearance of bones in graves.

The spread of herding did not erase earlier knowledge. Archaeologists studying the neighboring hunter-gatherer site Ust-Biyke-I and Nizhnyaya Sooru ask how local stone-tool traditions interacted with incoming pastoral practices. Their research treats this as an unresolved history of contact. People already living in the Altai were participants in the changes, not an empty space between migration arrows.

A small excavation at Nizhnyaya Sooru revealed a rectangular feature lined with stone slabs. Soot inside suggested a hearth, alongside pottery, stone tools and animal bones. Such traces bring us closer to the working spaces of a settlement than an elaborate grave can. The excavation was too limited to reconstruct a complete house or count its residents.

Stone remained useful even when metalworking was known. Wear on Nizhnyaya Sooru tools indicated woodworking; researchers also identified a tool for smoothing leather seams and grinders possibly used on metal. These were practical tasks behind shelters, containers and clothing. The investigators caution that early Altai Afanasievo metalwork was copper working, so the label Bronze Age should not make every implement bronze.

A broken pot could get another job. One of two clay spindle-whorl fragments at Nizhnyaya Sooru had been made from a potsherd. A whorl helps a spindle rotate when making thread. Reworking discarded pottery into equipment is a small, memorable example of household ingenuity; the find does not identify the spinner's age or gender.

Milk left an unexpected record on teeth. At early Afanasievo sites in the Mongolian Altai, researchers recovered sheep and other ruminant milk proteins from dental calculus, the hardened deposits on teeth. The study provides direct dairy-consumption evidence dated roughly 2912-2761 BCE. It does not identify a recipe for cheese or show that these early people already drank horse milk.

Meals differed across the region. A study of Altai human and animal remains found heavy reliance on animal protein and no clear evidence for routine fish consumption in the sampled people. Earlier results from the Minusinsk Basin suggested more fish eating. Sharing an archaeological label therefore did not mean sharing an identical menu.

The same Altai study found higher nitrogen-isotope values overall in males, which the authors suggest might reflect greater access to foods such as meat. That is a possible dietary difference, not a complete rulebook for family meals. Stable isotopes reveal long-term food patterns; they cannot tell us who served dinner or which child disliked it.

Narensu in northwestern Xinjiang lies south of the imported outline. A 2026 study found evidence of dairy consumption in its Afanasievo-period individuals and interpreted changing carbon-isotope values after about 2900 BCE as increased millet intake. This is a local dietary interpretation from human remains, not direct proof that every Afanasievo household grew millet. It complements the different results from the Altai.

sections.title: Families, health and what cannot be read

items.text: Ancient DNA can sometimes recover a family connection. At Afanasieva Gora, a published genetic study identified a woman, her son and her brother among the sampled remains. Their dates belong broadly to the early third millennium BCE. This is evidence of actual relatives within one burial community; it does not establish a universal household size or marriage system.

Disease also left microscopic evidence. A 2015 study identified DNA of Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, in two people from Afanasievo Gora dated within about 2900-2670 BCE. These infections long preceded the medieval Black Death. The findings do not reveal a medicine they used, the size of an outbreak, or whether disease ended an archaeological tradition.

At Shatar Chuluu in central Mongolia, excavated burial mounds had stone platforms edged with large boulders and pits beneath them. Small fragments of characteristic pottery helped identify the archaeological tradition despite few grave goods. Burial construction reveals coordinated effort and ways of remembering the dead, but does not by itself identify a chief, priest or set of funeral prayers.

No Afanasievo written artifact is securely available to reproduce. Genetic and archaeological connections with Yamnaya communities farther west help frame the language question. Researchers investigate possible Indo-European speech and a proposed relationship with much later Tocharian through comparison and archaeology. Those are historical hypotheses, not readable words left by an Afanasievo potter. No reconstructed phrase is presented here as an ancient inscription.

ending.text: There was no single Afanasievo kingdom to fall in 1500 BCE. Regional sequences changed much earlier: Okunev followed in the Minusinsk Basin, while Narensu shows later Khemceg and then Andronovo activity. Herding and dairying continued through changing communities. Neither a new archaeological label nor the map cutoff means that all earlier inhabitants disappeared.
